items.title: Show HN: A decent text-to-image model trained for ~$20K (Apache 2.0 Weights)
items.author: schopra909
items.content:
Pressure testing the Pyramid-JiT (P-JiT)

For us, this $21K training run is a proof-of-concept along the way to our next video model. We were surprised by how good the results looked given the size of the model, so we thought we'd share it with the world as an experimental release.

If you haven't followed our work previously, we'd love to take a step back and introduce ourselves. We're a 2-person research lab training our own generative video models entirely from scratch. The ultimate ambition is creative tools that democratize access to animation. You can read more about that .

Today, generative video models have two major flaws: they are too slow/expensive and they lack proper controls. Creativity is an iterative process. You make, you tweak, you get better. With this double whammy, video models (as they stand today) are effectively useless for storytelling.

When we set out to build Linum v3 earlier this year, the primary goal was to bring the cost envelope of inference down significantly. If our model is fast and cheap, it's the first step (of many) towards useful creative tools.

We've written extensively about the steps we've taken in this direction, but here's the long story short:

  • The bottleneck for training and inference for video is attention, O(n²). If we can compress more aggressively, we'll reduce the context window for attention, slashing the cost of training and inference.
  • Typically, compression is handled by a separate specialized model like a Variational Autoencoder, but that's not necessarily optimal. VAEs seem to have an empirical on the amount of compression they can achieve. More importantly, improving the VAE on its task of reconstruction can produce worse in the downstream diffusion model.
  • If you get rid of the VAE altogether, you should be able to compress more aggressively and learn faster. Diffusion models are a more powerful family of generative models than VAEs. We should be able to use them to compress and generate at the same time. Instead of using another model's latent space, the diffusion model should learn a latent space purpose-built for its use case. In turn, we should be able to squeeze more juice out of this compression.

In our last blog, we iterated towards a new architecture that we called the Pyramid-JiT (P-JiT). It's a pixel-space model that converges in 11× fewer samples than Linum v2 with 4× more aggressive token reduction (i.e., we represent a 512² image in the same number of tokens we used to represent a 256² image).

For the details on how we got there, we'd recommend you take a look at our previous blogs on and . But at a high level, we found a noise schedule for pixel-space models that helps the models better learn fine-grained detail. And, we added readouts along the trunk of the DiT.

Adjacent work in , , and all point to weak gradients in the early blocks of the DiT. By operating in pixel space, every block of our DiT is quite literally predicting a version of the final image, so we can boost gradient signal earlier in the network by predicting low-resolution versions of the final image. This helps accelerate convergence.

The architecture did well in our initial experiments, but we wanted to see how it performed when we trained it for longer (i.e., ~600M samples instead of 50–100M samples). It's a pressure test of sorts along the way towards larger models (and video).

Text and image each pass through two single-modality "refiner" DiT blocks, then merge into one stream of 22 identical DiT blocks. The text representation comes from a frozen Qwen3.5-4B model, which we read at layers 7, 15 and 27 (its three full-attention layers). We concatenate and project these representations into the text refiner. The image is split into 32×32 patches and compressed into a 1024-dimensional space, before being projected up into the image refiner blocks.

At block 5, we have a 2-layer readout that aligns the model's latent space to DINOv3-L. We have two linear readout heads along the trunk after blocks 10 and 16. As discussed earlier, these predict the clean image at a quarter and half resolution, respectively. The total loss is given by MSE at the readouts, PixelREPA cosine-distance, MSE at the final output head, and perceptual losses on the full resolution image ( and ).

Every DiT block is conditioned on the timestep through a low-rank AdaLN, following . The timestep embedding goes through one down-projection to 256-dim. Each block then has its own up-projection to a scale and a gate, zero-initialized so every block starts as the identity.

As described in our last blog, we employ a curriculum over the noise schedule. We start concentrated at high noise for the first 80M samples, so the model learns basic structure. Then, we widen the noise distribution for the remaining training time so it can learn fine-grained details. See Appendix A for details.

We start EMA at 100M samples, so the model has already learned decent representations of structure and detail. When we switch to 1024², we start with a fresh optimizer and resume training from the 512² EMA weights. At 1024² we double the noise scale from 2 to 4 to account for the redundancy of information (see JiT, Appendix ). The higher noise level and need to reproduce fine detail exactly at high resolution result in a higher overall loss, even as image quality improves rapidly. We use RoPE interpolation in the resolution transition. Moreover, we start the 1024² EMA 2M samples in, so it has adjusted to the new resolution before we start the averaging process.

It's still early days for post-training diffusion models

To be blunt, post-training is a very young discipline within diffusion models, and we've only seen the first sparks of it working in the past few months.

Of course there's been a lot of work in model and schedule distillation, but when it comes to post-training in terms of improving fundamental model capabilities (like we've seen with coding in LLMs over the past 18 months), it hasn't really come to fruition just yet for diffusion.

DPO has been around for a while, but tends to dramatically overfit to specific aesthetic choices. was one of the first articulations of bringing RLVR-style frameworks to diffusion, and that only came out last fall. Since then there have been a few papers like Diffusion and this June's (the best articulation of diffusion post-training so far, in our opinion).

We think that this difficulty in adapting techniques comes down to the fact that we don't have access to strong likelihood estimates in diffusion models like we have in auto-regressive LLMs. We'll dive more into these concerns and our full post-training stack in the coming weeks.

This model was not trained with images of rendered text (no infographics, PDFs, pages of books, PowerPoint slides), so it cannot write text or generate posters. As we detailed in our data filtration , we don't consider this data useful for our ultimate goal of animation tools, so this text-heavy data has been filtered out entirely from our dataset.

This is a small model (2B-parameter DiT, 4B text encoder), and accordingly there are a few areas where the model struggles: full body, many entities (e.g. 6 cars, crowds), multi-person interactions, and world knowledge. The model is capable of correctly generating these images on occasion. Training a larger model (e.g. 7B parameters) and further post-training would likely mitigate these issues.

Appendix A – Training Settings

items.title: Show HN: Kairos – Open-source risk and fraud decisioning platform
items.author: ayanb9440
items.content:
Hey HN, Ayan here from Finic. We’re launching Kairos, an open source alternative to Sift, Sardine, and other real-time fraud decisioning platforms. Kairos addresses two of the biggest problems facing traditional decisioning tools: a lack of labeled data to train on and dealing with fraudsters that are constantly changing their tactics.

1. Traditional fraud solutions use ML models such as XGBoost to detect fraud, but these models are dependent on quality labeled data which many businesses do not have. We address this by using “System One” decision models in additional to traditional models such as XGBoost and logistic regression. This allows you to incorporate plain language questions such as “Is this a throwaway email” into your decisioning, bypassing the need for large amounts of labeled data. This also allows you to capture aspects of fraud that are more unstructured, which is something that XGBoost models struggle with.

2. Fraud teams are facing off with live players that are constantly changing their behavior to bypass the detection logic they have in place. You can train a detection model or define a ruleset once, but it will become obsolete in a matter of weeks as fraudsters figure out what your detection logic is. This means that you need a team regularly training models and updating rules based on new fraud patterns. Typically this takes a large data science/ML team. Kairos addresses this by introducing an MCP server, so that your agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, etc.) can define a decision workflow, train models on your data, and pick the variant that performs best.

items.title: Show HN: A language model that lives in a boot sector
items.author: kerlenton
items.content:
All the ideas came from the boot sector demo scene where people had been writing chess and BASIC games in 512 bytes, even a C compiler. I wondered what one can do using a neural network instead of a program and generating boot logs for non-existent hardware was something fun to try.

Entire inference engine is 510 bytes of MBR, weights, vocab, and strings reside in the sectors following MBR. Small char-level neural network was trained on dmesg generated by machine, so machine produces Linux boot messages infinitely.

train.py performs precisely the same integer arithmetic operations as the asm code does and thus produces an output identical character-by-character to the one produced by QEMU. The difference analysis revealed my favorite bug. The characters at the beginning matched those generated by the simulator, but then the output diverged. I retrieved the hidden layer via QEMU’s debug port and compared the neurons' values with those of the simulator, one neuron at a time. Only the value of the first neuron was correct. The activation involves idiv, and idiv stores its remainder in edx. The pointer to the biases table was stored in edx, which resulted in the first neuron being biased correctly and the following ones using garbage. Now the bias' address is determined from the loop counter, and no pointers have to survive the division. Another bug I found simply by looking at the code before I did my first run-through: the BIOS print routine zeros out bx, but bx contains the predicted character number. This explains the push and pop of bx surrounding the print.

sectorllm is the most similar to my project, as it runs an actual 5-layer llama2 with attention mechanism in just 1.2K of assembly code. It is the trade-off in the opposite direction, as my engine needs to fit into one sector and therefore my network has just one hidden layer of int8 operations for dreaming the dmesg.

items.title: Show HN: Marelleo, an open-source story box I built for my kids using ESP32
items.author: foOg
items.content:
It started as an irritation on holiday

Last summer, on holiday with friends and a small tribe of children, I came across the Toniebox. And honestly, I thought it was great. The child puts a figurine on the box, the story starts. They take it off, it stops. No screen, no menu, no parent to go and fetch. A two year old gets it in one second, which is roughly the highest level of usability anyone can reach.

The gesture is perfect. The business model, much less so. All these boxes work the same way: the object sells for a more or less reasonable price, and the money is made afterwards, on the content. Whether it’s the Lunii and its closed catalogue, the Yoto and its card packs, or the Toniebox and its figurines, every new story is a purchase, from a catalogue I don’t choose, on an object I don’t control. You’re not buying a player, you’re buying a subscription dressed up as a wooden toy. And that genuinely annoys me.

Meanwhile, I had been telling myself for years that I wanted to do electronics. Not as a dabbler: actually understand it. Except I knew nothing about it. I own a soldering iron that comes out every three years to reattach a headphone wire, never to build anything. The kind of guy who knows what a resistor is without ever having had to choose one.

The two urges met in the car on the way home. That would be my project. An RFID reader, a tag, a box that plays an audio track depending on what you put on it. Not to make a product. Just for my kids, and to learn.

The breadboard, or the right to get it wrong

I already knew what I didn’t want. A Raspberry Pi is a full computer just to play an MP3: too big, too hungry, and it takes twenty seconds to boot. A child putting a figurine down does not wait twenty seconds, they wander off and play. At the other end, the genuinely low level chips, the ones you program in C with a 400 page datasheet, are far too steep for a beginner who would like to hear a story that same evening.

While reading around, I came across the two things that made the project possible. First the : a microcontroller with WiFi built in, beefy enough to decode MP3, simple enough to program like an Arduino, and sold for a handful of euros. Then the , that perforated plate where you push components in without soldering anything.

It sounds like a detail. It is the whole project tipping over. On a breadboard, getting it wrong costs nothing: you unplug, you start again, nothing is damaged. When you’re learning, that is exactly the property you need.

So I read documentation, I talked it through with Claude, I drew wiring diagrams in a notebook. And very quickly, far too quickly to feel earned, I had a circuit that played an audio track when you put a tag on it. It was ugly, a plate of copper spaghetti, the speaker lying bare on the table. But it worked. A few hours, and I had a thing that told stories. I don’t think I had been that pleased with something made by my own hands since childhood.

The potentiometer, the smoke, and the smell of ski wax

What came next is less glorious. To set the volume I added a potentiometer, that little rotary knob which is nothing more than a variable resistor. Except that wired wrong, it no longer sets anything at all: it becomes a plain wire between plus and minus. That has a name, it’s called a short circuit, and it heats up terrifyingly fast.

It smoked. And it gave off a very particular smell, which took me a good while to place before it hit me all at once: . Burning wax. I recognise it instantly now, and it is never good news.

The battery was the other piece of work, and the one that made me think. You don’t connect a lithium cell to two wires and move on. You need a charge controller, a dedicated chip that decides when and how to fill it, that stops at the right moment and cuts out before anything stupid happens. You also need to fasten it down properly, because a lithium battery rattling around inside an enclosure and getting pinched is precisely the scenario in those videos nobody wants to watch.

And then a stupid detail: my battery’s connector did not match the one on the charging board. Two little white plugs that look alike, two different pitches, incompatible. So I did what you do at eleven at night on a Tuesday when you’re nearly there: I cut the connector off and soldered the battery straight on.

Immediate consequence, which I had not seen coming: no connector any more, therefore no way to unplug anything, and no switch anywhere in the circuit. The box was . Twenty four hours a day. A lithium cell hastily soldered into an object that never turns off, sitting in a child’s bedroom. Written down like that, it needs no comment.

That is the moment I stopped treating this lightly. Not out of fear, but because I understood that I was no longer tinkering with a gadget on the corner of a table: I was placing an electrical object into my children’s daily life. Everything else in the project follows from that realisation.

From breadboard to perfboard

The first consequence was leaving the breadboard, and it wasn’t only about safety.

A breadboard holds by friction. Every wire is held by a tiny spring, which is wonderful for trying things and disastrous for lasting. Move the circuit and a contact is lost, and the fault that follows is far worse than a clean failure: it is intermittent. You hunt a bug in your code for an hour and a half, you reread the same function twenty times, and it’s a wire that no longer touches.

The next step is : the same grid of holes, but on a printed circuit, with every component soldered in. You lose the right to be wrong, you gain a circuit that holds together. That’s where I really learned to solder, and above all where I understood that my repair soldering had nothing to do with manufacturing soldering. Repairing is remaking a joint that existed. Building is making a hundred in a row, all clean, all identical, knowing that the hundred and first is the one that will fail.

My kids unscrewed the knob until the wires tore off

For the enclosure I got very lucky: lent me his 3D printer and helped me through the first attempts. Without him I would still be cutting cardboard with a ruler. I drew my models in Fusion 360 on the free hobbyist licence, and printed.

The first version was too big and too fragile. And quality control arrived faster than expected, in the shape of three children aged 21 months, 5 and 7.

They broke the knob by turning it like animals. The volume knob ended up spinning with no end stop, round and round, and as it turned it wound the wires around themselves until it tore every one of them off. I opened the box onto a little nest of twisted copper. That’s where I learned the most important rule of the entire project: a five year old does not turn a knob, they unscrew it. And they don’t stop when it resists. They stop when it gives.

So I started over. I took every measurement again with callipers, component by component, so that each hole would land exactly where it should and each part would be held by plastic rather than by its wires. I thickened the walls, added pockets, lowered the height. Version after version, the object stopped looking like a prototype and started looking like an object.

Still in the spirit of nothing being allowed to give, I also abandoned self tapping screws. Screwing straight into printed plastic holds once, twice, and on the third go the material splits along the layers: the hole holds nothing any more and the part is fit for reprinting. The real answer is called a . You set it on the hole, come down on it with the tip of the soldering iron, the brass heats up, melts the plastic around itself and sinks in. As it cools you have a metal thread captured in the part, which you can screw and unscrew a hundred times.

And then came the only test that no technical argument passes on my behalf: Not politely: she put it on the living room shelf, among the objects you don’t tidy away when someone rings the doorbell. That also settles the cube shape, which I wasn’t sure about. An object for children that you don’t need to hide is an object that ends up being used.

In the opening photo, all of that is still visible: a circle engraved on the top, which says where to put the figurine because the antenna sits right underneath, the volume knob beside it, the play button, and the name raised in the front wall. The figurines are painted wooden people with an NFC sticker glued under their feet. Any object would do: a toy car, a token, a flat pebble. The child decides what tells what, and that is exactly what I wanted.

I wanted nothing left dangling

At that point I had a version that worked pretty well. But a wired circuit, however well soldered, is still a wired circuit. There is always a cable pulling on a joint, a module hanging off its legs, a connector that works loose when you shake it. And I had just spent a few weeks measuring, very empirically, how much my children shake things.

So I changed category and set about designing a . Everything that was scattered, brought together on a single board: the power supply, the charger, the amplifier, the SD card reader, the connectors. Every part in its place, nothing moving, nothing sticking out.

I used Claude to go from my wired circuit to a clean schematic, and that is where the division of labour became interesting. It reads a datasheet very well, spots that a pin needs a pull-up, works out a value, fetches a footprint from the library rather than copying it from memory. But it cannot route. Routing, that is to say physically drawing the path of every copper track between components without ever crossing another, is something I did by hand, in KiCad. Entire evenings spent moving lines by a tenth of a millimetre to squeeze a connection between two pads eight tenths apart.

That file has to be gone over with a magnifying glass before you send it, for a very concrete reason: you don’t order a single board. The minimum is five, manufactured and assembled in one go. One mistake in there isn’t a touch-up job, it is five boards for the bin and the whole invoice.

So I had it reread the entire schematic, line by line. It found three things I would never have seen, and each one would have cost the order.

The three mistakes caught before the order

The resistor that would have killed everything. To produce the 3.3 V the processor needs, I use a step-down converter, and I had put two resistors around it forming a divider. That is the normal way to set the output voltage. Except the chip I had picked comes in two families: an adjustable one, and a one. I had taken the fixed one. With my divider, the regulation would have read a voltage far lower than reality, concluded the output was too weak, and pushed. The arithmetic gives 13.7 V on a rail meant for 3.3. The WiFi module, the SD card, the NFC reader: all dead within a second of power-up.

The diode the wrong way round. In KiCad, pad number 1 of a diode is the cathode, and my file placed it the other way round. A reversed diode at that spot means the 5 V doesn’t come out, so the 3.3 V doesn’t exist, so the board doesn’t start at all. Five mute boards in one go, with no way of noticing without having them made.

And the checker that checked nothing. KiCad automatically verifies that tracks respect minimum clearances. Mine was configured with a minimum clearance of . It ran, it reported zero errors, and it approved absolutely anything, silently. That is the worst kind of bug: the tool that reassures you.

Once, the roles reversed and it gave me a silly amount of pleasure: was the one who spotted that two components in my bill of materials were out of stock, before it did. We turned that into a small program that queries the manufacturer’s catalogue and returns the stock and price of each part number, so that it never happens blind again. A part number is not a given: you recheck it on the day of the order, not the day before.

160 euros of boards, and nothing happens

I ordered from JLCPCB, who manufacture the board and populate it. For 160 euros I got five, already assembled, enough to keep one and give the rest to cousins and friends. Opening that parcel was one of the very good moments of the project. Green boards, crisp, components perfectly aligned, my name written on them, out of a file I had drawn on my sofa.

First contact with the manufactured object: I can’t plug the USB in. The factory had added a small strip of material under the socket, a breakaway tab used to hold the board during assembly, which you’re meant to snap off on arrival. I had to work up the nerve to break it by hand on a thirty euro board. That took me a good ten minutes of contemplation.

Then I plug it in and test. And nothing happens. The NFC reader’s LED blinks, but no figurine is recognised, nothing plays, nothing appears on the network. Nothing.

I spent a quarter of an hour telling myself I was an old fool who had just burned 160 euros on useless boards, and that it served me right. A genuinely bad moment. Then I went looking, methodically, unplugging the harnesses one by one.

The culprit came down to two wires. I had swapped the two middle conductors on the NFC reader’s ribbon, the ones carrying the serial link. That link always crosses over: what one transmits, the other has to listen to. Wired straight, both ends talk at the same time and nobody listens. The module powers up, its LED blinks away happily, and it never answers. It is the kind of fault that looks serious and is just carelessness.

And the best part comes last. I had fixed the cable, and it still didn’t work. For two stacked reasons: first, the program questions the reader , so until you restart, the repair is invisible. Second, the power switch cuts nothing at all while USB is plugged in, because it acts on the battery’s transistor and USB feeds the board by another path. So I was spending my time “restarting” a board that wasn’t restarting, to test a repair that was already done.

Cable finally unplugged and plugged back in, the long awaited line dropped onto the console:

bibliotheque : 4 figurine(s)

And for thirty seconds I thought it was still broken, because I couldn’t hear anything. The volume knob had been left at the bottom of its travel, at minimum. There is a poetic justice in ending a day of debugging on a volume problem.

But other than that: the board worked first time, with no rework at all. Not a single flying wire, not a track to scrape, not a resistor to replace. For a first board designed by someone who didn’t know what a footprint was three months earlier, I really did not expect that.

All that was left was to assemble everything into the enclosure, this time for good.

“Dad, we’ve already heard that one”

That remark is what set off the entire software side, and it brings us back to the starting point. A box with a frozen catalogue, even a catalogue of my own, becomes exactly the problem I wanted to avoid. The content had to belong to us, and it had to be able to change with no tool, no cable, and no me.

Everything goes through a web page, because there is no screen

The box serves its own page. You type its address into a browser, from a phone or a computer, and you see the figurines, the stories present on the SD card and what is playing right now. Nothing to install, nothing to update, no account.

For the very first start-up it opens its own WiFi network. A phone that connects to it brings up the setup page on its own, exactly like in a hotel: the box answers its own address to any domain name question, which makes the phone open the page without being asked. You pick your network from a list, type the password, it joins the house and closes its own network behind it.

The first version did that over Bluetooth. It worked, but it needed a dedicated app, which is untenable for an object you’d like to give away, and the Bluetooth stack weighed , nine per cent of everything the chip has, to be used exactly once in the life of the box. I threw it out without regret.

You send files from the page, they land on the SD card, you associate them with a figurine. A figurine carries as many tracks as you like, in whatever order you like, and they play through to the last one without looping. That opens everything up: recording your own voice to tell the kids a story when you’re away, putting on the songs they ask for on repeat, dropping in whatever you find online. MP3 and M4A, the two formats that come out of a phone or a Mac without converting anything.

One figurine, one URL, and it’s a radio

A track doesn’t have to be a file. You can give a figurine a , and the box connects to it and plays the stream as it arrives, storing nothing. It opens the connection, receives the audio in small pieces, decodes them and sends them to the amplifier while always keeping a few seconds in reserve, to absorb the network’s hiccups. If the connection drops it retries several times before giving up, because a home WiFi has its holes and a two year old should not have to understand why the music stopped.

So my children have radio stations that look like little wooden people, and I find that very satisfying.

And it updates itself over WiFi

This is the part I’m proudest of, because it solves a problem specific to finished objects. The box is screwed shut, assembled, sitting in the living room. If I want to fix something, I’m not going to take it apart every fortnight. So it fetches its new versions on its own.

It queries a fixed address, written into the program and deliberately impossible to change from the network. That is a security choice: a box that accepted being told where to look for its software would accept being made to install anything, and someone on the same WiFi would be enough.

If a newer version exists, a button appears in the page. It downloads it into a , the one that isn’t running, checks the fingerprint of the file it received, and only switches over if everything is intact. A power cut in the middle of a transfer therefore never leaves it mute: at worst it restarts on the old version, as if nothing had happened.

The safety net, and the time it would have been useless

That leaves the nightmare of a closed object: a version that starts correctly but whose networking is broken. It is valid, the box switches to it, and there is no longer any path to fix it. Hence a : a freshly installed version has to prove it can connect. Three start-ups without ever seeing the network, and the box goes back to the previous one by itself, before it even turns its radio on.

A version I had published was reopening its setup portal even though it knew the house network perfectly well: it was reading its saved credentials too early, before the radio had started, and concluding it had none. I had nothing to do. After three start-ups it went back to the previous version on its own, and I could repair it at my leisure.

Same family of mistake, funnier: each box opens a network carrying the last four digits of its hardware address, so that two boxes in the same house stay distinct. Except I was reading that address before the radio started, at which point it answers six zeros. Every box in the world would have been called Marelleo-0000.

And once, the net could have done nothing at all. My publishing script was only compiling one of the two hardware variants, the prototype. The printed board would have received the other one’s image: audio and SD card pinouts swapped, memory looked for on the wrong bus, and a header announcing 16 MB of memory on a chip that has 8. The worst part is that the trial period would not even have caught it, since the WiFi itself would have worked perfectly. It would have gone deaf and blind while believing itself in good health. We found that just before pressing the button.

One last anecdote, for anyone the detail amuses. One day the update started failing with no error message at all: the transfer would start, make progress, and the box would restart suddenly, in silence. Now, a silent failure says a lot. No error means the program had no time to write one, so it didn’t stop, it was interrupted. The download task had 8 KB of stack, and I had put a 4 KB buffer in it. There was nothing left for the encrypted handshake of the secure connection. The silence itself was the clue.

Three kids, three uses I hadn’t planned for

This is the best moment of the project, and it was in no specification. Each of them made the box their own, and none of the three ways is the one I had imagined.

Her music playlists on one figurine, her stories on another, and podcasts about insects. She chooses, she asks for additions, she runs her own catalogue.

Stories. Lots of stories, chained on a single figurine through to the last track, and replayed until I know them by heart.

Her lullabies, and her toddler podcasts live. Thank you France Inter and Radio Pomme d'Api.

One figurine, one gesture, and each of them has their own box inside the same box. That is exactly what I was after at the start, and it arrived through software rather than through a catalogue. The difference fits in one sentence: nobody sells me the content, and nobody can take it away from me.

I bought a 3D printer and built a workshop in the basement

There is one consequence I hadn’t foreseen, and it isn’t about the box.

I was starting to seriously abuse François’s kindness, since his printer had produced every one of my enclosures. And above all, I was enjoying all of this far too much: the evenings, the weekends, perfectly indefensible hours spent getting obsessive about a two millimetre fillet or the depth of a pocket. I decided this would not be my last electronics project, because I genuinely love it. So I bought a Bambu Lab A1.

I told myself it was a useful purchase: spare parts you stop rebuying, toys you repair instead of throwing away, custom storage. All of that is true. It wasn’t the reason.

And I installed it in the living room. A machine half a metre across, which blows, vibrates, runs for fourteen hours at a stretch and smells of hot plastic, in the middle of the room where Marceau is learning to walk. At the time it seemed perfectly reasonable. I was shown the door in no uncertain terms, and entirely deservedly: you do not install a production unit in a living room.

So I ran a network line over the mains down to the basement and set up a print station there. And it is frankly better than I imagined: I start a print from the sofa, it runs in the dark two floors below, and I go down to collect the part the next morning. No more noise and no more smell of hot plastic upstairs, and a living room that stays a living room. The fifth version of the enclosure came out of there. It’s the one in the opening photo.

The three enclosure parts to print, the board’s manufacturing files ready to drop into JLCPCB along with the bill of materials and component positions, the firmware source, and documentation that starts from zero: what to buy and for how much, what order to go about it in, the pinout of the module version, and the traps that cost me evenings. All MIT licensed, so do what you like with it.

You can start with the breadboard version, without soldering once, and only order the board if you catch the bug. That’s the path I took, and the one I’d recommend: the breadboard is the place where being wrong costs nothing.

And there are two ways to use it. Rebuild it as is, following the files, and get the same box my kids have. Or take it as a starting point: a different enclosure, a different speaker, different buttons, the code changed to your taste. Only one thing to know in that case, and it’s written in large letters in the repository: the firmware is written for that exact assembly, the pinout lives in the code, and a wire moved means a line to change. I flagged it because it is exactly the sort of detail that has you hunting a fault for an evening.

If you build one, I’d really like to see it.

From , the French word for hopscotch, the game where you move forward by putting a foot down on a square. But mostly from ceau, a and Lnie, to whom the box belongs.

Thanks to François Lagunas for the printer, the advice and the patience. And to my wife, who has lived for months with this project spread across evenings and weekends, and who said yes to the printer before I could get a single argument out.

items.title: Show HN: Hob - Open-source, on device alternative to Claude Cowork and ChatGPT
items.author: pancomplex
items.content:
Hey HN, I'm Christian and this is a new OSS project I've been noodling on for the last couple of weeks. Hob is a free, MIT-licensed desktop app for Mac, Windows and Linux that works on your files the way the Claude and ChatGPT desktop apps do, except the model runs on your own computer. It uses open-weight models (currently Gemma 4 and gpt-oss). All your chats and files never leave your system. The only things that go online are web search (can be turned off in settings) and any MCP connectors you add yourself.

- Automatically finds the best open-weight model for your hardware on first install (Mac/Linux/Windows)

- Writes sandboxed Python code for ad hoc tools (data processing, document conversion, graphs etc.)

- Built-in web search (powered by SearXNG)

- CRUD to your local filesystem

- Works fully offline with no internet

Before building this I tried every local AI app I could find, but it seemed each one had different problems. The main thing I noticed is that none of them could do what the ChatGPT and Claude apps do with your files, e.g. read and change files in a folder, look at images, run code in a sandbox, draw a chart. The most advanced thing any of them did was paste a plain text file into a small context window, which basically failed as soon as you had a file larger than a few KB. I couldn't find anything that could easily parse images and bigger PDFs.

The OSS solutions that were more advanced all seemed to default to hosted models (either OSS or closed), which defeats the entire point of the privacy that on-device OSS offers. They also seemed to push towards an account/open-core style business.

I build it using Electron bridged with llama.cpp in its own process. On initial load, the system will try and figure out if you have a compatible graphics card and if not default to CPU-only (I ran into a lot of issues of graphics card beeing seemingly compatible but then crashing on first query, there's a whole saga to this lol). Code execution happens in a sandbox that can only write to the chat's folder and has no network unless asked (sandbox-exec on macOS, Landlock on Linux and a low-integrity process on Windows). Images go to a small Qwen3-VL model. Dictation is a local Whisper model.

The hardest part was definitely to get the smaller models to use tools reliably. Ran into a ton of issues of 4B models happily saying "here's your chart" without ever calling the chart tool or get stuck in an infinite call loop. I spent a fair amount of the work building guards vs tweaking prompts (that didn't really work for small models).

I understand the pushback that local models are weaker than frontier cloud models. This is true, but for most tasks for most normal people, I'd argue you rarely need the newest frontier model. From my own evals, systems with 16+ GB of RAM do really well, and if you have a GPU or more RAM, you get very close to what you'll get out of the box with a frontier hosted model.

Excited to hear what you think and see how it runs on other systems!

items.title: Show HN: Hurston-1 open source TTS that speak Southern American and Afro-English
items.author: Gcarter08
items.content:
Accented English text-to-speech built for the phone, steered by a plain-language voice description.

Hurston-1 introduces : text-to-speech made for the phone line, where most customer service still happens, even when the other side is an AI agent. It learned in part from real phone calls between our contributors and AI voice agents, and its phone mode delivers what a caller actually hears: 8 kHz G.711 audio, ready for Twilio and other telephony systems. Full 24 kHz audio is still the default.

Hurston-1 is a fine-tune of Maya1 (Apache-2.0) built by Destined AI to speak English accents that most TTS systems handle poorly: Southern American, Nigerian, West African, East African, Southern African, alongside broader American English. It is the first open model in Destined AI's ClarityVoice family.

pip install torch transformers snac soundfile scipy speechbrain   
python hurston.py --model . --check \
    --accent  --gender Female \
    --text  --out hello.wav


python hurston.py --model . --check --phone \
    --accent  --gender Male \
    --text  --out call.wav

 hurston  Hurston, describe
tts = Hurston(, check=)          
wav = tts(, describe(, , ))

In 1995 André 3000 stood on stage at the Source Awards, in front of a crowd that booed OutKast, and said "the South got something to say." We think that line still fits.

Hurston-1 was built in Atlanta by a small, independent team. Since 2021 we've been recording consented, paid contributors from the American South and from across Africa. These are voices that most AI systems still flatten into generic American English. Nobody handed us a funding round to do this, so we built it ourselves. These voices belong in AI, and now they have an open model.

We named it for . She grew up in Eatonville, Florida, trained as an anthropologist, and traveled the South recording how Black Southerners actually talked: their stories, songs and speech, at a time when few institutions thought those voices were worth keeping. Our work is a small echo of hers. The name is a tribute; it does not imply any endorsement by her estate.

A few lines the way people actually talk around Atlanta. All synthetic; every voice is generated from a description.

"The South got somethin to say."Male, Southern American accent, clear conversational
"Meet me on Peachtree. No, not that Peachtree, the other one."Female, Southern American accent, casual conversational
"I'm fixin' to head out, traffic on 285 is already backed up."Male, Southern American accent, casual conversational
"What part of Atlanta you from?"Female, Southern American accent, casual conversational

More samples for every accent are in (descriptions and text in ).

The model was trained on descriptions of the form Gender, age, accent, style, pace:

, , , Nigerian (Yoruba) English accent, Nigerian (Igbo) English accent, West African English accent, East African English accent, East African (Swahili) English accent, Southern African English accent
clear conversational voice, casual conversational voice, clear audiobook narration voice
, , ,

Pace labels are absolute speaking rates learned from the natural voices in training data: roughly slow is under 2 words per second, measured 2 to 2.6, natural 2.6 to 3.4, fast over 3.4. The model follows them approximately, not exactly. It still highly matches the behavior of the underlying dataset.

Each call samples a new voice that fits the description. Note: Hurston-1 does not clone voices and was not trained to reproduce any real person.

Most voice AI is demoed in studio quality and then deployed over a phone line. Hurston-1 is built for where it will actually be heard:

  • About 10 hours of the training audio (7,600 turns from 250 contributors) is phone-quality speech from real calls with full-duplex AI voice agents, alongside studio-style reading and conversation.
  • (or ) filters the output to the 300 to 3,400 Hz telephone band, resamples it to 8 kHz and encodes it as G.711 mu-law ( for A-law), the formats phone networks, SIP and Twilio use. It is a channel effect applied after synthesis, so still judges the full-quality take.
  • returns raw mu-law bytes, the payload Twilio media streams expect.
 hurston  Hurston, describe, ulaw_encode
tts = Hurston(, check=)
call = tts(, describe(, , ), phone=)
payload = ulaw_encode(call)

Some places to start. At Destined AI we use accented TTS like this to build broad, high-quality test data, and that is still the use we would point to first.

  • Test data for speech recognition. Generate the same sentences in nine accents and see where your ASR, captioning or transcription system breaks. It makes a quick accent-coverage check or a regression set before a release.
  • Simulated callers for voice agents and IVR. Pair Hurston-1 with an LLM that writes caller scripts (customers, patients, applicants) and run hundreds of synthetic calls through your agent before real people do. Use phone mode so the agent hears what it will hear in production. Good for catching where an agent mishears accents, names or numbers.
  • Training data augmentation. Add accented synthetic speech to ASR, keyword-spotting or wake-word training sets where those accents are thin. Mix it with real speech instead of training on synthetic audio alone.
  • Voice prompts and announcements. Phone menus (phone mode output drops straight into an IVR), appointment reminders, store and transit announcements, app onboarding, in a voice that sounds like the community you serve.
  • Listening practice across world Englishes for learners, and accent-familiarity practice for customer service, healthcare and call-center staff.
  • Accessibility and read-aloud. Read articles, forms or messages aloud in a voice closer to home.
  • Games, animation and media drafts. Background characters, temp voice tracks and podcast or audiobook drafts, labeled as synthetic.
  • Accent-fairness audits of speech systems, listening and perception studies, and benchmarks that cover voices most datasets leave out.

one consistent brand voice across sessions (each call is a new voice; see Limitations), cloning a specific person, or anything safety-critical without a human listening first.

Two questions: does it sound like the accent, and does it say the words?

Accent strength vs base Maya1. Base Maya1 documents five accents (American, Indian, Middle Eastern, Asian American, British). For a fair comparison we prompted it in its own documented description style, naming each accent, and compared it with Hurston-1 on the same 10 sentences and 18 voices (180 clips per model). An accent classifier (African vs American English, trained on real speakers) scored each voice group:

Accent (probability judged African)
Southern American (should be low)

The classifier cannot tell Southern American from general American English; that accent was checked by listening.

Whisper large-v3-turbo word error rate (WER) against the input text, numbers normalized (lower is better).

(the same 180 clips as the accent test above, , single take):

(30 unseen sentences × 17 voices, 510 clips):

The harder set covers reading, health, customer service, names and numbers, expressive and long sentences. Base Maya1 is very clear because it mostly stays in American English; Hurston-1 keeps nearly the same clarity while actually doing the accent.

Accent (510-clip set, WER with )

Names and numbers are the hardest category (WER 0.17 with ). Part of that is the recognizer misspelling African names such as rather than the model mispronouncing them.

Median 2.84 words per second with , against 3.76 for base Maya1. Hurston-1 speaks a little more deliberately; use for quicker delivery.

Testers heard the same sentence from base Maya1 and Hurston-1 in random order, without knowing which was which, and chose the one that sounded more like a real person with the requested accent. Hurston-1 was chosen of the time and base Maya1 ; the rest were rated a tie or neither (54 comparisons). Base Maya1 was never chosen for an African or Southern American voice; its few wins were on plain American English.

LoRA (rank 64) fine-tune of Maya1, 2,000 steps, about 190 hours of speech:

Destined AI accented English corpus: scripted reading, conversational speech and ~10 h of real phone calls with AI voice agents, from consented, paid contributors~136 (a slice of our 1,800+ hour corpus)
LibriTTS-R (audiobook style, keeps general quality)

Accent labels come from each contributor's self-reported background, checked against an audio accent classifier and human listening; speakers whose audio and labels disagreed were relabeled or removed. Pace labels come from each clip's measured speaking rate. All contributors were adults. The full Destined AI corpus (1,800+ hours, recorded since 2021) is not included in this release; contact us about licensing it.

  • No voice consistency across calls. Each call is a fresh voice that fits the description. Long text is split at sentence ends into chunks of about 40 words, so the voice can change between chunks. Consistent named voices are planned for a later release.
  • Names, dates and amounts are the weakest content. Use and listen before you ship anything important.
  • The generic label is weaker (WER 0.26); use a specific region instead.
  • English only. No child voices.
  • Like other autoregressive TTS models it occasionally produces a garbled or overlong take, or the voice shifts mid-take; catches most of these.
  • Output is leveled to the same loudness for every voice, and pauses longer than half a second inside a take are shortened.
  • Phone mode changes the channel, not the speaking style: the model does not yet choose call-style delivery (turn-taking, backchannels) on request. See What's next.

Hurston-1 is the first step. What we are building toward:

  • A model that learns to like a person on a call, not just sound like the phone line: a call style distinct from reading style, with natural turn-taking, "mm-hm"s and call pacing, learned from our recordings of real people talking with full-duplex AI agents.
  • The same named voice across every call and every sentence, for agents and brands.

Do not use Hurston-1 to impersonate real people, deceive listeners, or commit fraud. Tell listeners when speech is synthetic. Audio in is synthetic.

  • Model weights: Apache-2.0, derived from by Maya Research (Apache-2.0).
  • Audio codec: 24 kHz by Hubert Siuzdak (MIT), downloaded at run time. Phone mode uses ITU-T G.711 (public standard).
  • Optional checking: by OpenAI (MIT) and from SpeechBrain (Apache-2.0), downloaded at run time.
  • Training data: LibriTTS-R (Koizumi et al., 2023; CC BY 4.0), Mozilla Common Voice (CC0), and Destined AI's own corpus.

items.content:
I was pretty terrible at singing, now I’d say I’m bad but not terrible. This is because I’ve been using a singing app (won’t name it here) that scores me on my pitch and timing throughout the song so that I can improve.

Lately however, the app I’ve been using has flooded their song list with songs that aren’t originals. I didn’t like this at all as for me, it’s easier to try to improve when you’re singing along to the original.

So, I asked an agent (Claude Code) if it could write some code to listen to Spotify and also listen to me and see if it could detect both pitches and score me. It impressed me by writing some Python and showing me my pitch in the terminal!

It couldn’t go all the way though and detect the singer’s pitch in real time.

So I found the next best setup and built OnKey, a Mac app that needs to listen to the song once (it doesn’t save it) and then when it’s learnt the song (takes a couple of minutes), you can sing along to the pitch track that it’s learnt. OnKey is free to use and open source under the MIT license.

It can listen to Spotify, Apple Music, and YouTube playing in your browser with the right permissions.

During the build I found that someone had done something similar in Nightingale, but this requires a library of songs exported to disk and who has this in 2026 (maybe some of you ;) - but we need to help the normies too).

The app sends out to find the song info (short Shazam fingerprint, and looks up song details), lyrics (from LRCLIB), and checks for updates.

The app never sends the music (it doesn’t save this to disk) and your voice. Everything you’d expect to stay private does.

It’s still weak in a few places:

- when the song’s backing is noisy it’s hard to pick the pitch track out

- sometimes it gets a note an octave off

- it’s limited to Apple Silicon Macs, M1 or later, and only macOS 14.2 up because extra drivers aren’t required past this point

- the scoring is built for beginners like me so it’s fairly easy on you

Would love for people to try it out and let me know what works and what doesn’t for them!

items.title: Show HN: Omnara – Open-source alternative to Claude Managed Agents
items.author: kmansm27
items.content:
Hey all, Kartik from Omnara (https://omnara.com) here. We're building an open-source API for running durable agents. You create an agent with an API call, and Omnara runs the agent loop, gives the agent sandboxes to run commands in, and handles secrets, permissions, and RBAC. Each agent's state is stored in Postgres, so agents survive restarts and cost nothing while idle. You can message them and stream their events over the API.

You may remember us from our early days, when we made a remote-control phone app for Claude Code and Codex. Since the harness ran on a laptop back then, we had to build a relay to reach it, it stopped when the laptop closed, and moving it to a cloud sandbox meant syncing code and agent state between machines. We didn't think remote-controlling a local agent was end-game for how people would run agents, so we built a new product where the agent runs in the cloud, any client can talk to it through an API, and it can still use your laptop as one of its machines.

Anthropic and OpenAI are building hosted versions of this, like Claude Managed Agents and the OpenAI Agents API. Omnara is an open-source version you can run on your own servers and use your own models. It's basically a harness server like the opencode or codex servers, but durable, scalable, with the usual harness features like file and shell tools, subagents, compaction, permission prompts, MCP, skills, memory, yada yada yada.

Here's some interesting architectural decisions we made while building this out:

Most harnesses, like Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, Goose, etc, run the agent loop in one long-lived process that keeps its log in a JSONL or SQLite file. In Omnara, the log is an append-only event log in Postgres, with inputs, model outputs and tool calls stored as typed rows in their own tables. The loop runs on stateless workers in the control plane. A worker runs one iteration of the loop, either a model call or the tool calls it produced, then releases the agent and puts the next iteration on a queue in Postgres. Whichever worker is free picks it up, so each iteration of an agent's loop can run in a different process on a different machine. Each iteration's result commits in one transaction, so the model output, its tool calls, usage and the next wakeup are saved together or not at all. If a worker dies mid-iteration, nothing commits, its lease expires, and another worker retries it. Agents waiting on a user, a tool or a retry don't hold a worker, so one worker can multiplex thousands of agents.

Also unlike other harnesses, the machines that the workers (our agent loop) run on aren't where the agent runs its commands. Instead, any macOS or Linux machine with an internet connection, like your laptop or any cloud sandbox, can run a small daemon (omnarad) that connects out to Omnara, so it doesn't need any open inbound ports. The agent then gets tools for that machine, like running a command or editing a file. An agent can have any number of machines connected to it. A fun thing I like to do is I have my laptop and a cloud sandbox connected to the same agent, so when my laptop is on, my agent codes there and I can interact with it, and I have it often push to Github. When I close my laptop, my agent sees the laptop went offline, pulls the latest changes to its cloud sandbox, and continues there.

items.title: Show HN: Uberblok – an interactive museum of ZFS internals
items.author: storagebits
items.content:
How does ZFS find its data after a crash?

A pool holds millions of blocks spread over several disks. After a crash, ZFS has to find the last consistent state of the pool without reading all of them. It starts from one small record on each disk, the uberblock. ZFS writes changes in batches called transaction groups (txg), one every few seconds. The uberblock holds the number of the last txg and a pointer to the top of the pool’s tree of blocks. Every other block can be reached from that pointer.

ZFS never writes a new uberblock over the current one. Each disk keeps a ring of slots for uberblocks, and each txg writes its uberblock to the next slot. The previous uberblock stays intact in its own slot, so a power failure during the write still leaves a good one on disk.

When the pool is imported, ZFS reads every slot, sets aside the ones that fail their check, and uses the valid uberblock with the highest txg.

The figure shows one ring. Press Next txg to commit one txg: the new uberblock takes the slot after the previous one, and the previous one stays in its slot. When animations are on, the ring also commits a txg every 1.3 seconds by itself, and Next txg stops it. Change the sector size of the disks. A slot takes one sector, and never less than 1 KiB, so the same 128 KiB ring holds 128 slots on disks with 512-byte sectors and 32 on disks with 4 KiB sectors.

Every uberblock starts with the same magic number, , read aloud as “oo-ba-bloc”.

The figure follows three places in the OpenZFS source. Open a Source note to see the lines, taken from release .

starts with a magic number and the on-disk version. It also holds the txg, the time of the sync and , the block pointer to the pool’s own metadata, from which the rest of the tree hangs.

picks the slot: the txg modulo the number of slots. The txg grows by one at each sync, so the uberblocks go round the ring and the newest one never lands on the one before it.

On import, runs once for every slot read. It ignores a slot whose read failed or whose magic number is wrong, and keeps the uberblock that compares highest.

What the figure leaves out

The figure shows one ring. A disk carries four labels, two at its start and two at its end, each with its own ring, and every txg writes the same slot in all four. The ring is often said to hold 128 uberblocks. That is true only for 512-byte sectors: it holds 128 KiB, so 64 slots at ashift 11, 32 at ashift 12 and 16 from ashift 13. With one slot is kept for MMP. The txg numbers are made up.

items.title: Show HN: I built a task system to handle the drudgery so I could focus on tasks
items.author: dmayle
items.content:
I'm a software engineer from the east coast (who has lived in Boston, NY, the bay area, UK, France), and I built a task system called 3 & Done. It's the place you trust to store everything you need to do. It accepts voice input for rapid entry, as well as text (it stores the audio locally so you can listen to jog your memory) and emails you every morning with the three most important things for you to do that day, and why, based on what you've said about the task: deadlines, urgency, sitting too long.

I've been at software engineering for about 44 years now... Grew up with it, which was unusual when I started, and I was always good about getting into the zone and doing things. The career started small, small company, then back office, the dot com startups, then smaller companies again after the bust, a non-profit, and eventually YouTube (Google at the time, but just barely) and Meta (just Facebook when I was there).

When I hit the startups, and later big tech, it was no longer enough to just be an engineer, to have drive, to be good, you had to be organized, you had to follow through, get stuff done, and that's where the task systems started. Twenty-five over the years (and yes, I've actually counted), from Moleskine notebooks with Getting Things Done, evernote (remember evernote?), bug trackers, todoist, asana, google keep, among others.

When I managed on the Facebook News Feed, I got into gantt charts (for me and my team), spreadsheets, OmniPlan... I remember apologizing to my director for being so disorganized (because I felt I was making a mess of it), and he told me that I was the most organized engineer he knew.

That was because I was doing all of the work in the background, the trimming, the sorting, the reviews, but it was just so much work. Which was why I changed from system to system. Each time it built up, and I had to spend more time looking at things I couldn't or didn't get done, when I was rushed and couldn't put time into today's review, it would pile up, and then using it was so much work that I would start taking mini-notes, just emailing myself a few things to do the next day.

That's actually the thesis of the app (but not where it started), that if I could just have a few things to do emailed to me each day, I could get it done.

This app actually started when I described my previous startup failures into a Claude web session, and it repeated back to me what I had just said. My previous failures were because I spent too much time building the stuff I needed, and not building what I was supposed to be building.

I decided that the app would email me three things to do every day (which matches best practices for attention), but that the day was always yours to decide. We won't overload you, but you can add more, if you're feeling up to it, or cut back, and we never shame and try our best not to nag (I often only finish two). If we get it wrong, you can tell us, and we'll re-rank it once a day, or you can set it manually, and if you do, we never override that choice. The web app is live, and native for both platforms is coming. In the meantime, on Android, you can use gestures to quick launch into the voice input so saving a task is only a gesture away (e.g. double-tap the back of a Pixel, double-press the power button on Motorola).

Now let's talk about the dirty parts. I used AI to help me build this. Anthropic models mostly, and the brains of the app come from Anthropic models (I like the quality, I like the privacy, absolutely no training on customer data, and the stance of the company). This app is not some one-shot wonder where I asked frontier models to build a task system and then I put it on a server to show you.

I have prompts for the various features (e.g. ranking, generating suggestions, task extractions), I have eval sets of task lists (not anyone's real tasks, but constructed from patterns in my tasks, or the tasks of testers who allowed me to fix the problems they were having), with the three I expect to come out. I store the eval outputs, and re-test whenever I add a new rule to a prompt, or whenever testing a new model version. The great thing about having this eval set is that it catches when I get it wrong. When I introspect a failed run, sometimes it's because I need to tune a prompt, but sometimes it's because I missed something in my own ranking.

I did the same thing with my infrastructure as well, so this time, instead of setting up servers, and building login systems, and managing databases, I built on Vercel (git push to serving Next.js), Neon (hosted postgres).

I started getting emails mailed to me by mid-June, but started getting usable suggestions on June 26, and I've been using it every morning since. I wanted it to be easy to get started, and easy to use, so the input handles mess (you can add multiple tasks in the same run-on sentence, and a friend who helped me test it just pasted his entire obsidian todo list in wholesale to get started).

I wanted to make sure that anyone could try it out, so I built a trial feature that uses the real in-app ranking with a list of items you provide.

If you want to try the service, there's a free 14-day trial (card required), and then it's $99/year or $9.99/month after that (plus sales tax). We warn you seven days before your card is charged and if you cancel, you keep access through the term (either the trial, or our last paid period). Online, through settings -> billing, no email, no call.

I really hope you'll try it out. If you do, please tell me if we did a good job picking out your day.

items.author: thedracle

Hi HN!

I’m Jason Thomas, one of the founders of CoScreen.

As some of you may know, Datadog sunset the CoScreen service on July 31st.

Four of us from the original CoScreen team have spent the last couple months building a free and open source pair programming tool inspired by those that came before us: It’s called Petal (https://github.com/kiruna-labs/petal)

Some history first, because when we started CoScreen we had hoped to break the sad and established pattern of this industry.

Screenhero was an exceptional tool that a lot of us loved for pairing. Multiple cursors, low latency, you could click your partner’s editor, and just start typing. It felt like magic while we had it. Then Slack bought it in 2015, and shut down the standalone app in December 2017.

When Till, Max, and I started CoScreen, we were aware of this history, and wanted to build an even more magical collaboration and screen sharing experience: the entire concept was “throw a window from your laptop up on someone else’s screen, and start collaborating with zero friction.”

Datadog acquired us in 2022, and thus began the great adventure of adapting our real-time technology into Datadog products, while also continue developing CoScreen as a standalone tool from the Datadog ecosystem. Datadog invested in the product for years and we’re thankful for that. But CoScreen itself proved, like so many other screen sharing tool acquisitions, to be too tangential from the customer base and core mission. We instead built other communication features in Datadog, the integrations with other video platforms, and also its wildly successful MCP server. We weren't the only ones. Around was bought by Miro and shut down in March 2025. Multi (formerly Remotion) was acqui-hired by OpenAI in 2024 and shut down about a month later. It's nearly always the same story: a small team builds something hard that people love, a platform buys it for the team or the feature, and the standalone product doesn't survive the integration. So we decided firmly to do things differently this time. Petal is completely free and open source and we aren't monetizing it. If we lose interest or get hit by a bus, you can self-host it or fork it, and nobody can sunset it on you. Honestly it's a love letter to everyone in this community that supported us, believed in us, and to liberate collaborative screen sharing from this vicious cycle.

We hope through this we can help foster a large and vibrant community around innovating in this product sector. What Petal does: shared windows show up as real windows on your desktop, movable and resizable, not tiles in a grid. Several people can share at once, everyone gets a labeled cursor, and you can click into any shared window to type and scroll. Rooms are persistent, so you click once to join "eng-sync" instead of passing links around. It runs on macOS and Windows (Linux is next, this time for real and you can help us!), plus a web app. Media goes over LiveKit. You can use our hosted instance with zero config, or point the app at your own LiveKit server with one docker-compose if you want the traffic to stay on your network or even use an entirely different video backend if you want to. The part that still feels strange to us: CoScreen took almost six years to build. The first version of Petal took under eight weeks, from scratch, with frontier models like Fable and Astra doing a lot of the work. Real-time video and window capture is some of the most unforgiving code we have ever written, so we didn't expect that. We will do a proper writeup on what worked and what didn't, and are happy to answer questions about it here. Till, Darren, Max and I will be in the thread.

I felt there are not enough consumer apps that run locally with no calls to the outside world that help us manage sensitive corners of our lives. This app in its local variant only downloads a couple of models and occasional updates, it does not send any analytics nor data.

Features-wise, Pulse local is a complete budgeting app that offers an assistant built on top of a fine-tuned model and thousands of rules embedded in the code itself. I'm sharing it for free with options to help me continue experimenting with fine-tuning and expanding along this direction.

How it works: you import a CSV from any bank, in any currency. When you ask a question, a tuned Qwen3 0.6B model reads it into a structured query, and code, not the model, does the money math against the ledger. A 4B checker model double-checks each money answer; when the two readings disagree, the app says it is not sure instead of guessing. That change took wrong answers from about one in five to 5 in 494 questions across our last three tests. The write-up covers how we test, the designs that failed, and the limits of the claim: https://pulseos.finance/pulse-local/writing/agree-or-not-sur...

The tuned weights are on Hugging Face (PulseOS/pulse-local-qwen3-0.6b).

Limitations: the first start downloads about 2.9 GB of models. With the checker on, a money answer takes 12 to 14 seconds (you can turn the checker off). Small models can still misread an open-ended question. The app answers in English. Mac only for now; Windows is next.

The app is free. An optional Connected mode (Sync Pass, $29/year) syncs US banks through Plaid; transactions pass through our server's memory and are not stored.

Existing benchmarks measure solve rate and token output/cost, but don't punish excess code, which makes a codebase harder to work with in the long term. I wanted to measure this since it matters most for long-term projects.

GPT-6 and Claude 5.5 have no public patches yet, so I ran them myself on 3–10 tasks on my own subscriptions (shown as faded circles, not ranked).

Hi HN! I'm Saarth. I'm in 9th grade, and I built Atticus.

Atticus is a fast and cheap Mac assistant that can do tasks for you. You hold down Control-Option-Space, speak or type your task, be it complex or a simple browser search, and Atticus will get on it.

The interesting part is that simple tasks, like opening apps, playing a Spotify playlist, or web queries, don't touch AI, and instead are processed locally and typically finish in under a second. Any tasks that are more complicated will be sent to Claude via claude -p, meaning you never need an API key and Atticus will run on your existing Claude Pro or Max plan. By using this approach, costs are also cut down immensely, with, on average, tasks costing a fraction of a cent.

To achieve Atticus' speed, it remembers shortcuts from each task it completes. When it does a task right for the first time, it saves its steps and replays them the next time without AI. For example, a workflow of creating a new meeting took about 30 seconds the first time around. Atticus then logs the exact steps to memory and takes 5-8 seconds on the next pass. To add to this, Atticus also learns about you as you use it more and from what's on your computer, including your name, your apps, and things you want it to remember, personalizing its answers to you.

To combat the safety concerns over giving an AI unrestricted access to your device, Atticus has toggleable restrictions, so before anything is deleted, sent, bought, or written to a file, the user is prompted before that action.

Some features I'm currently working on include a meeting copilot that capitalizes on Atticus' speed, allowing Atticus to listen in on meetings and answer questions in real time as they come in, personalized to the context of the meeting and what it knows about you.

To run Atticus, macOS 26 or higher is required for its voice transcription features. The voice transcription is also done locally by macOS.

Atticus is free, open source, and also very fresh, and I'm completely aware of its many rough edges, which is why I'd love to hear from everyone about what breaks and what you guys would like to see Atticus do!

items.title: Show HN: Apogee: Rebuilding Mozilla's Orbit, fully local and private
items.author: zxdc7896
items.content:
Hey everyone!

Last year, Mozilla released Orbit, an AI-powered browser summarizer hosted on a GCP server. After people started digging into the extension, they discovered things like backend endpoints such as store_result. Eventually, Mozilla discontinued the project.

For the past month, I’ve been trying to rebuild Orbit from scratch, but with one major difference: Apogee is fully local and privacy-focused. Apogee doesn’t send or store your data. It can directly connect to your local Ollama instance for inference. I’ve also added WebGPU integration for Chrome and Transformers.js for Firefox to provide faster, local responses.

It can summarize: Articles and websites, YouTube and Billie videos, Wikipedia articles ,Hacker News and Reddit threads.

Install Apogee:

Chrome: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/apogee/pgemlpomhkdc...

Firefox: https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/apogeeext/

Obviously it is far from complete. Would love to hear your feedback and suggestions!

items.title: Show HN: Jevman – AI decision models play Pac-Man
items.author: felix089
items.content:
Openai just launched their decisions endpoint, cloudflare launched clef the other week, and many more jev alternatives are out there.

We wanted to put the popular ones to the test and thought Pac-Man is a good benchmark for simple and fast decision making.

So we let jev 1.13, kev, clef, clef flash, GPT-6 Luna and Laya play Pac-Man against bot ghosts.

The low latency of these models allows for real time play. We had each model play 100 games, published a leader board and open-sourced the repo so anyone can run their own model and join the ranking. Link to repo: https://github.com/opper-ai/jevman-benchmark/blob/main/CONTR...

You can also join the game and play as Pac-Man yourself, and the ghosts are the models, either a mix of models or all jev, kev, clef etc. A game costs about 2 cent, all models are running via my startup opper, and we added free credits for everyone to try.

It's pretty fun to play and surprisingly difficult to beat jev's highscore. Any feedback is more than welcome!

items.title: Show HN: Proton Drive for Linux
items.author: khaosdoctor
items.content:
Hello everyone, I wanted to share this small project that I have. It's born out of a necessity that I had, because Proton doesn't ship a Linux version of the drive yet (it's apparently coming out later this year but who knows?) and all the current solutions are hacky and wonky at best. But for the time being I really needed to mount my Proton drive on my Linux machine the way I mounted it on my Mac, so I (and my faithful AI slave) did this small utility that allows you to mount your Proton Drive in a FUSE FS like if it is a local folder.

It's fully written in Go because Proton's drive SDK and API libs are all in Go, and there's a community project on top of the reverse engineered proton API there too. I am not a Go developer, I know the foundations, so of course I used AI quite a lot, I am not super proud of it, but I am using it daily and testing it myself for a few months before releasing here.

Hope you like it, feedbacks are welcome, just please be mindful of the person on the other side :)
